title: US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

sheetTitle.es: La esclavitud y la trata de esclavos en EE. UU., 1850

summary: Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.
subject: History
unit: Reform and the road to war
alsoFits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

layers.name: US States and Territories 1850
layers.shows: States and territories in four legend groups: Free states; Free states and territories by compromise; Slave states; and Slave states and territories by compromise. Each pop-up is titled with the state's name and says whether it allowed slavery and from what year.
layers.source: Traced from a map in Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), as the pop-ups say

layers.name: Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade
layers.shows: Solid black lines along which enslaved people were forced to move within the United States, with no arrows; dashed and dotted lines in the same layer are sea routes and the voyages of the Amistad and the Creole. No pop-up.
layers.source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920)

layers.name: Underground Railroad Approximate Routes
layers.shows: Approximate routes that freedom seekers took north to the free states and Canada, as orange lines. No pop-up.
layers.source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), an early-1900s interpretation

layers.name: Cities
layers.shows: 69 towns and cities along the Underground Railroad routes, from Virginia and Kentucky to Ontario and Quebec, as dots with name labels that appear when zoomed in. No pop-up.
layers.source: Traced from Harper's Atlas of American History (1920)

layers.name: Missouri Compromise Line
layers.shows: The line at 36°30′ North set in 1820. Its pop-up gives the line's name, the year it was enacted and a note on what it divided.
layers.source: Not stated on the layer (hosted by the MapMaker team)

layers.name: US 1850 Original Map
layers.shows: A scan of the 1850 map that the other layers were traced from. No pop-up.

knownIssues.note: The line "It is recorded on the primary source as:" shows a code number (for example 11) instead of the map's own wording.
The layer has separate West Virginia and Oklahoma features. In 1850 West Virginia was part of Virginia (it became a state in 1863; its pop-up year is 1863), and Oklahoma was not a state or territory.
Missouri is drawn twice, as two overlapping features: once under Slave states and once under Slave states and territories by compromise. Clicking it gives a pop-up that says 1 of 2.

Some pop-up years can puzzle students: Illinois gives 1848 (its new constitution, though it entered as a free state in 1818), Maine gives 1783 (when it was still part of Massachusetts), and New Jersey has no year, so its pop-up reads oddly.

compellingQuestion.en: How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo dividía la esclavitud a Estados Unidos en 1850?

questions.task: Use the legend for US States and Territories 1850 to tell the four groups apart (free, free by compromise, slave, slave by compromise), name a state in each, read two states' years from their pop-ups, and find the eastern line between free and slave states. The layer draws West Virginia separately and Missouri twice, so this question asks for groups and examples, not a count.
frontOfClass: Open the legend and show the four groups for US States and Territories 1850.
Click Pennsylvania and read its name and year in the pop-up.
Click Virginia and read its name and year.
Click Iowa, then Texas, and match each shade to its legend group.
Ask: which groups are free and which allow slavery?
Ask: where in the East does the shade change from free to slave?

student.en: Open the legend and find the four groups for US States and Territories 1850. Which groups are free and which allow slavery? Click a state in each group to read its name, and click two states to read what year each became free or slave. Where is the line between free and slave states in the East?
student.es: Abre la leyenda y busca los cuatro grupos de la capa US States and Territories 1850 (estados y territorios de EE. UU. en 1850). ¿Qué grupos son libres y cuáles permiten la esclavitud? Haz clic en un estado de cada grupo para leer su nombre, y en dos estados para leer en qué año cada uno se volvió libre o esclavista. ¿Dónde está la línea entre estados libres y esclavistas en el Este?

answer.where: Legend for US States and Territories 1850: four groups. Following the legend shades, the Free states group has 14 states; Iowa and California sit in the paler Free states and territories by compromise group. The Slave states group has 15 as drawn, counting West Virginia; Texas sits in the paler Slave states and territories by compromise group, and Missouri is drawn twice (once in each slave group), so accept 14 to 16 free and 14 to 16 slave with reasons. Pop-up title gives the state name; the first line gives the year (for example Pennsylvania 1780, Virginia 1788). In the East the shades change along the southern border of Pennsylvania and then the Ohio River.

table.caption: States by legend group on the map, 1850
rows: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin
Free states and territories by compromise
Iowa and California, plus Oregon, Minnesota and the unorganized territories
Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia (part of Virginia in 1850), North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, Missouri

answer.text: Historically there were 15 free and 15 slave states in 1850 (Iowa and California free, Texas slave). The legend groups split them by how they became free or slave, so the counts students get depend on which groups they add together; the reasoning matters more than the number.
answer.accept: One state correctly named for each of the four legend groups; two state years read from pop-ups; the eastern line described as the southern border of Pennsylvania and then the Ohio River. Do not mark on counts: the layer's groups make a count ambiguous.

questions.task: Find the Missouri Compromise Line (gray dashed) and click it for its pop-up. Which slave state lies mostly north of it, and why does that matter?
frontOfClass: Zoom out until the gray dashed Missouri Compromise Line shows across the West.
Click the line and read its pop-up: the name and the year enacted.
Point to Missouri, just north of the line.
Ask: which slave state lies mostly north of the line?
Ask: why does that matter?

student.en: Find the Missouri Compromise Line (the gray dashed line) and click it to read its pop-up. What year was it enacted? Slavery was banned north of it in the Louisiana Territory. Which slave state lies mostly north of the line, and why does that matter?
student.es: Busca la línea del Compromiso de Misuri (la línea gris discontinua) y haz clic en ella para leer su ventana emergente. ¿En qué año se aprobó? La esclavitud estaba prohibida al norte de ella en el territorio de Luisiana. ¿Qué estado esclavista está mayormente al norte de la línea, y por qué importa?

answer.where: Missouri Compromise Line pop-up: title Missouri Compromise Line (36°30′ North), year Enacted 1820, and a note that the line divided future slave and free states west of the Mississippi and that Missouri was the exception because most of it lies north of the parallel. On the map, Missouri (green, slave state shades) sits almost entirely north of the line.
answer.accept: 1820; Missouri. A good answer says Missouri was allowed in as a slave state even though it lies north of the line, so the line was a deal, not a rule that applied everywhere, and it set up the argument over every new state and territory. Mentioning Maine as the free state admitted at the same time is extra.

questions.task: Follow the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade (turn Underground Railroad Approximate Routes off in Map layers to see them clearly). Click the states where the lines begin and where they come together to read their names. Where do the lines reach the coast? The lines have no arrows, so students infer the direction from the pattern and what they have learned.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn off Underground Railroad Approximate Routes.
Point to the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade.
Click Virginia, where several lines begin, and read its name.
Click Louisiana, where the lines reach the coast, and read its name.
Ask: the lines have no arrows; from the pattern, which way were enslaved people forced to move?
Ask: what else do you know that supports your answer?

student.en: In Map layers, turn off Underground Railroad Approximate Routes so the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade stand out. Click the states where the lines begin and where they come together to read their names. Where do the lines reach the coast? The lines have no arrows: from the pattern and what you have learned, which way were enslaved people forced to move?
student.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), desactiva Underground Railroad Approximate Routes (rutas aproximadas del Ferrocarril Subterráneo) para que resalten las líneas negras continuas de la capa Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade (rutas internas de la trata de esclavos). Haz clic en los estados donde empiezan las líneas y donde se juntan para leer sus nombres. ¿Dónde llegan las líneas a la costa? Las líneas no tienen flechas: según el patrón y lo que has aprendido, ¿en qué dirección fueron obligadas a moverse las personas esclavizadas?

answer.where: Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade, solid black lines (no pop-up). Reading them against the state pop-ups: several lines start in Virginia (one from near the Ohio border and one from Kentucky join them), one starts in North Carolina, and they run south and west to meet in central Alabama and at the Mississippi coast in Louisiana. They reach the coast at New Orleans and the Gulf (Louisiana, Alabama) and on the Atlantic off South Carolina.
answer.accept: A good answer names Virginia (and Kentucky or North Carolina) at one end and Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, with New Orleans on the Gulf, at the other, and says the lines join up as they head south and west toward the ports. From that pattern and from class, students should say enslaved people were moved from the older Upper South to the Deep South and the Gulf, where cotton and sugar plantations wanted labor; accept any direction argued from the map plus a reason.

questions.task: Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark and follow the orange Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River; the Cities labels appear when zoomed in. Where do they lead, and why do many continue to Canada?
frontOfClass: If Underground Railroad Approximate Routes is off, turn it back on in Map layers.
Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark.
Zoom in until the Cities labels appear along the orange routes.
Trace one orange route north from the Ohio River to Lake Erie.
Ask: where do the routes lead?
Ask: why do many keep going past the free states?

student.en: Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark. Follow the orange Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River, and zoom in to read the names of the towns along them. Where do the routes lead? Why do you think many keep going past the free states?
student.es: Abre el marcador Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio. Sigue hacia el norte, desde el río Ohio, las rutas anaranjadas del Ferrocarril Subterráneo, y acércate para leer los nombres de las ciudades a lo largo de ellas. ¿A dónde llevan las rutas? ¿Por qué crees que muchas siguen más allá de los estados libres?

answer.where: Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes (orange lines) and Cities (orange dots in the US, black dots in Canada; labels draw when zoomed in). Routes run north across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Lake Erie and the Detroit River, at Cleveland, Ashtabula, Toledo and Detroit, and on to the black dots at Chatham and Toronto (Ontario) and Montreal (Quebec).
answer.accept: North to the Great Lakes and across into Canada. A good answer gives two or three town names from the map and explains that freedom seekers were not safe in free states (after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 they could be captured and returned), so Canada, outside the United States, was the safer end of the route.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch that marks free and slave states and one route (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

objectives: Use the legend to tell free states and slave states apart, including those set by compromise, and locate the eastern line between them.
Read the year each state became free or slave from its pop-up, and the year of the Missouri Compromise Line from its pop-up.
Explain why Missouri, a slave state lying mostly north of the Missouri Compromise Line, was an exception.
Trace the internal slave-trade routes from Virginia to the Gulf coast and the Underground Railroad routes north to the Great Lakes and Canada, naming states and towns from the map.
Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how slavery divided the United States by 1850.
discussion: The slave-trade routes have no arrows, yet you worked out which way enslaved people were forced to move. What on the map told you, and what did you have to bring from outside the map?
Many Underground Railroad routes keep going past Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Canada. What does that tell you about what 'free state' meant in 1850?
These layers were traced from a 1920 atlas. What might a map drawn today show differently, and why does that matter when we use old maps as evidence?

differentiation.support: Do question 1 together from the front and write the four legend groups on the board, with one example state next to each, before students start on the pop-ups.
differentiation.stretch: Turn on US 1850 Original Map in Map layers and compare the scanned 1850 map with the traced layers: what did the tracers keep, and what did they leave out?

resources.title: Avenues of Escape on the Underground Railroad

beforeYouStart.en: By 1850, the Northern states had ended slavery or passed laws to end it, but in the South slavery was legal and growing. More than 3 million people were enslaved in the United States. Each time a new state joined the Union, Congress argued over whether slavery would be allowed there.
beforeYouStart.es: Hacia 1850, los estados del Norte habían abolido la esclavitud o aprobado leyes para abolirla, pero en el Sur la esclavitud era legal y seguía creciendo. Más de 3 millones de personas estaban esclavizadas en Estados Unidos. Cada vez que un nuevo estado se unía a la Unión, el Congreso discutía si allí se permitiría la esclavitud.

readingTheMap.en: States and territories are shaded brown if they were free and green if they allowed slavery; the paler shades mean free, or slave, because of a compromise. Open the legend to see the four groups. Click a state to read its name and year in the pop-up. A gray dashed line marks the Missouri Compromise Line; click it for its pop-up. Solid black lines are internal routes of the slave trade. They have no arrows. Dashed and dotted lines in the same layer show sea routes and the voyages of two ships, the Amistad and the Creole. Orange lines are approximate Underground Railroad routes. Zoom in to see the towns along them: orange dots in the United States, black dots in Canada.
readingTheMap.es: Los estados y territorios aparecen en tonos marrones si eran libres y en tonos verdes si permitían la esclavitud; los tonos más claros indican que eran libres, o esclavistas, por un compromiso. Abre la leyenda para ver los cuatro grupos. Haz clic en un estado para leer su nombre y su año en la ventana emergente. Una línea gris discontinua marca la línea del Compromiso de Misuri; haz clic en ella para ver su ventana emergente. Las líneas negras continuas son rutas internas de la trata de esclavos. No tienen flechas. Las líneas discontinuas y punteadas de la misma capa muestran rutas marítimas y los viajes de dos barcos, el Amistad y el Creole. Las líneas anaranjadas son rutas aproximadas del Ferrocarril Subterráneo. Acércate para ver las ciudades a lo largo de ellas: puntos anaranjados en Estados Unidos y puntos negros en Canadá.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about slavery in 1850 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre la esclavitud en 1850 que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: Only US 1850 Original Map is off when the map opens (the scanned source map, worth comparing with the traced layers). For question 3, students turn Underground Railroad Approximate Routes off so the slave-trade routes stand out. The states layer draws West Virginia (a state only from 1863) and draws Missouri twice, so question 1 asks for the legend groups and examples rather than a count.

misconceptions.claim: Freedom seekers were safe once they reached a free state.
misconceptions.response: After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 they could be captured in free states, which is why many routes on the map continue to Canada.

misconceptions.claim: The Underground Railroad was a real railroad.
misconceptions.response: The routes on the map are paths people walked, rode or sailed, with help along the way; the name borrowed railroad words.

misconceptions.claim: Every Northern state banned slavery at the same time.
misconceptions.response: The pop-ups give a different year for each free state.
